newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan group says anti-Japan protests won't stop.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan group says anti-Japan protests won't stop.

text.p: Angry activists vowed on Thursday to impeach Taiwan government officials who forbade them to make a protest flight to an East China Sea archipelago held by Japan but claimed by Taipei and Beijing.
"It's an international joke that we can not even fly to our own territory," said National Assembly member Fung Hu-hsiang, head of the organising Protect-the-Diaoyus Alliance.
"We won't go tomorrow, in part because of the bad weather, but that's not the end," Fung told Reuters by telephone.
"We will not stop until we can get to the Diaoyus."

The alliance had hoped to mark the 51st anniversary of Taiwan's 1945 return from a half-century of Japanese colonial rule on Friday by dropping flags on the deserted islands claimed by Japan as the Senkakus and Taiwan and China as the Diaoyus.
But Taiwan itself blocked the protest on Thursday.

A multi-agency task force "recommended that the government not allow Protect-the-Diaoyus people to rent helicopters to go to the Diaoyu islands based on the national interest and the people's safety", vice foreign minister Cheng Wen-hua said.
Taiwan aviation authorities were complying with the recommendation, state-funded television said.

Seeking to ease disappointment over the scuttled protest and appease anger over recent Japanese moves to assert sovereignty, the task force recommended that Taipei press Tokyo for further negotiations on the issue.

"We will...seek to impeach the communications minister, the foreign minister, the defense minister and even the premier as they failed to protect the country," Fung said. "We cannot allow Japan's militarism. Our anti-Japan mission will continue."
Japanese ultra-rightists sparked a nationalistic backlash from Chinese across Asia after raising Japan's flag and building a lighthouse on the islands in July to assert Tokyo's claim.
Taiwan fishermen complain that Japanese patrol boats have barred them from fishing waters near the islands.

On October 7, Taiwan and Hong Kong activists vowing to take the islands back broke through a Japanese maritime cordon and planted flags of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China and the arch rival communist People's Republic of China.
Tokyo voiced regret for what it called the illegal landing and vowed to take necessary measures to stop similar actions.
Japan took the islands and Taiwan as war booty in 1895 after defeating imperial China and refuses to acknowledge that the dispute is open for discussion with China or Taiwan.
Two rounds of Japan-Taiwan talks, unofficial due to their lack of diplomatic ties, have failed to defuse the situation. Japan recognises only the Beijing government, Taiwan's rival.
Foreign minister John Chang said on Wednesday that Taipei would host a third round on fishing rights and other issues stemming from the sovereignty row. He gave no dates.
China and Taiwan, themselves split in 1949 by a civil war, say the islands have been Chinese for centuries and should have been handed back after Japan's defeat in World War Two.
